encounters.cc: Progressive swelling and deformity of right foot over past 8 months with mechanical grinding

lines: Progressive swelling and deformity of right foot over past 8 months with mechanical grinding

The patient presents for evaluation of progressive right foot deformity in the context of longstanding Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus with severe peripheral neuropathy, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and acromegaly followed in Endocrinology since 2020.
He states that the foot has been “changing shape” and that he sometimes hears cracking or grinding when he walks, but feels little to no discomfort.
He reports that approximately nine months ago, he twisted his ankle while walking on uneven pavement but continued his daily routine because the pain was minimal.
Since that time, the swelling has gradually worsened, and the foot now looks “crooked” to him.
His wife reports that he sometimes walks with an unusual gait but does not complain of pain.
- Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (20-year duration, poorly controlled)
- HIV infection (diagnosed 10 years ago, on intermittent antiretroviral therapy)
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
He has a history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus for 20 years and peripheral neuropathy diagnosed 5 years ago.

The patient works as a delivery driver and spends many hours standing or walking each day.
He often wears old, worn-out work boots.
He has not had any fevers, chills, or recent infections.
Review of systems is otherwise unremarkable.
On physical examination, the right foot appears markedly swollen, warm, and erythematous with obvious midfoot collapse and deformity.
There is joint instability, bony crepitus on palpation, and reduced active range of motion.
Achilles tendon reflexes are absent bilaterally.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ bilaterally.
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, are within normal limits.
Plain radiographs of the right foot demonstrate bone fragmentation, joint subluxation, and sclerosis consistent with advanced joint destruction.
There is no joint aspiration performed as there are no signs of infection.
